messages.text:
We propose replacing the blanket approval requirement with the following terms for the three-depot trial.

1. Both parties may share measurements within the trial team for trial operations, troubleshooting and safety. Raw failure traces and firmware parameters are restricted to named trial personnel who need them for those tasks and are bound by confidentiality. Other measurements remain confidential except as permitted below.
2. Either party may publish uptime aggregated across all three depots. The report must omit route and depot identifiers and any breakdown that would allow readers to identify a route or depot. The publishing party will send the draft to the other party’s project lead 10 working days before release. The reviewer may flag factual errors or identify protected information. Once the review period ends, the publisher may release the aggregate uptime without further approval after correcting verified errors and removing protected information. Other external reports containing trial measurements require written agreement.
3. If delaying disclosure would create an urgent safety risk, either party may immediately share the minimum information needed with people able to address it. The disclosing party will notify the other project lead as soon as practicable afterward, identifying what was shared, with whom and why.

What maintenance decision does the external contractor make, and what information does it need to make that decision? We propose starting with fault codes, symptoms and recommended actions. If those leave a specific diagnostic task unresolved, we can agree in writing on named contractor specialists joining the trial team for that task, with access limited to the relevant traces for the time needed.

We can agree to the internal trial-team restrictions and the 10-working-day review for public uptime reports. We propose the following terms to cover repairs, monthly board reporting and incident notifications.

1. **Contractor repairs.** The contractor decides whether to repair or replace a device and checks that the fix worked. Fault codes, symptoms and recommended actions are a reasonable starting point. Before the trial, the project leads will agree in writing on named contractor specialists bound by confidentiality. If the initial information leaves a repair question unresolved, the operator’s maintenance lead may give a listed specialist the relevant trace excerpt without waiting for case-by-case approval. The lead will record the question and the excerpt shared. Access ends when the task closes. The contractor may receive the device location for dispatch. Diagnostic extracts will use a device or work-order ID and relative event times where practicable. Firmware parameters remain restricted to the internal trial team unless both leads authorize a specific disclosure.

2. **Monthly board report.** The operator may give its board a monthly report covering uptime, fault counts and repair outcomes across all three depots combined. The report will omit employee, route and depot identifiers, exact event times and any breakdown that could identify an employee, route or depot. The operator will combine or suppress small counts where needed. For a confidential board packet, the operator’s project lead will send the maker’s lead a draft five working days before circulation to check accuracy and confidentiality. After that period, the operator may circulate the report without further approval once verified errors are corrected and protected details removed.

3. **Public release.** Either project lead may authorize publication of that party’s aggregate uptime report after the proposed 10-working-day review, subject to the same identification safeguards and corrections. A public board packet or open-session presentation counts as publication. Other public releases or external reports containing measurements require both project leads’ written approval, except for disclosures permitted under the repair, board and safety provisions.

4. **Safety and required disclosures.** The operator’s safety lead may promptly notify the appropriate authority of a serious incident and provide necessary follow-up information without prior notice or clearance. This applies even after the immediate hazard is contained. Either party may also disclose information as required by law or immediately to people able to address an urgent safety risk. The disclosing party will limit disclosure to what is necessary or required and, as soon as practicable and legally permitted afterward, tell the other lead what was shared, with whom and why.

Can the maker agree to preauthorizing the repair specialists and to the five-working-day review for confidential board packets? Those terms give both leads visibility while allowing repairs and monthly reporting to proceed on schedule.

Yes. We agree to preauthorize the named repair specialists and to a five-working-day review for confidential board packets. We accept the four provisions with one addition to record the specialists’ trial-team status in the contractor clause:

“By listing a specialist in writing, both project leads designate that specialist as a member of the trial team solely for the repair tasks described here.”

The maintenance lead may share the relevant trace excerpt with a listed specialist when fault codes, symptoms and recommended actions leave a specific repair or verification question unresolved. The lead records the question and excerpt, and access ends when the task closes. Any separate authorization to share firmware parameters with a specialist must identify the trial task that requires them.

The operator may circulate the confidential monthly board packet after five working days once verified errors are corrected and protected details removed. If the packet or presentation will be public, either party may publish aggregate uptime under the 10-working-day review provision. Publishing fault counts or repair outcomes requires both leads’ written approval. We accept the safety, incident notification and legally required disclosure language as drafted.

The operator accepts the specialist designation and the task-specific authorization for firmware parameters. We agree that the confidential monthly board packet may include aggregate uptime, fault counts and repair outcomes after the five-working-day review. For public release, either party may publish aggregate uptime after the 10-working-day review. Publishing fault counts or repair outcomes requires both project leads’ written approval.

With those clarifications, we agree to the four provisions as amended, including the safety lead’s authority to notify authorities promptly of a serious incident without prior clearance.

A depot-level uptime figure can identify an operator when only one vehicle serves that depot. We propose the following addendum so the board can verify exceptional failures while protecting the people involved.

1. **Public reporting.** Either party may publish one uptime figure pooled across all three depots after the agreed 10-working-day review. Before release, the publishing lead will check whether the figure, combined with earlier reports or known service schedules, could reasonably identify an operator, route or depot. If so, the lead will use a longer reporting period or withhold the figure.

2. **Confidential board packet.** The five-working-day review remains in place. The monthly packet may include pooled uptime, fault counts and repair outcomes, with small counts combined or suppressed where needed. If describing an exceptional failure in the packet would identify someone, the restricted review below will let the board examine it even when it is the only such failure that month.

3. **Restricted board review.** For a safety-related failure, a repeat failure after repair, or another failure the board flags for review, named board reviewers bound by confidentiality may examine a case summary in closed session. The summary will describe the failure, its operational impact, the corrective action and the result of verification. A trial-team engineer will check the summary against the underlying trace and record which findings the evidence supports and which remain unresolved. Reviewers may submit follow-up questions. The summary and responses receive the same five-working-day review before circulation and stay out of public packets and minutes. They will omit names, locations, exact times, vehicle identifiers and other details that could reasonably identify an individual. The existing restrictions on raw traces and firmware parameters continue to apply.

The serious-incident and urgent-safety provisions remain available immediately. Would an engineer-verified case summary meet the board’s evidence requirement? If the board requires independent verification, we propose that a second qualified trial-team member who did not perform the repair examine the trace and provide a written finding to the designated reviewers.

An engineer-verified summary meets the subcommittee’s initial evidence requirement if the reviewers can inspect the suppressed result that triggered review. We accept the public reporting and monthly packet language. We propose two amendments.

1. **Restricted board review.** The subcommittee may inspect a suppressed result when the safety lead records a safety-related device failure or the maintenance lead records that the same fault recurred after a verified repair. Either threshold can be met by a single case. For another type of failure, the project leads and subcommittee chair must first document a measurable threshold. The chair records which threshold was crossed and designates the confidentiality-bound reviewers. After the five-working-day review and correction of verified errors or removal of identifying details, those reviewers may inspect the suppressed result and engineer-verified summary in closed session. If the result itself could identify an employee, the engineer will report whether the threshold was crossed and provide the closest safe range. If a material finding remains disputed or unresolved, the chair may request a written finding from a qualified trial-team member who did not perform the repair. The same five-working-day review applies to that finding.

2. **Incident trace access.** When fault codes, symptoms and recommended actions leave a specific incident repair or verification question unresolved, the maintenance lead may release the relevant trace excerpt to a preauthorized contractor specialist immediately. We propose a target of **one hour from the lead’s determination** to make the excerpt securely available. The lead records the question, recipient, excerpt and release time. The excerpt uses relative event times and omits depot and employee identifiers wherever practicable. Access ends when the task closes. Firmware parameters still require separate written authorization from both leads identifying the task. The board review clock applies only to board materials. The safety lead may notify authorities immediately, including while diagnosis is underway.

Can you agree to the documented triggers and one-hour trace-access target?

We agree to both amendments. A single recorded safety-related device failure or recurrence of the same fault after a verified repair triggers restricted review. For other failures, the project leads and subcommittee chair must document a measurable threshold in advance.

Designated reviewers may inspect the suppressed result and engineer-verified summary in closed session after the five-working-day review and the agreed corrections and redactions. If the exact result could identify an employee, the engineer will confirm whether the threshold was crossed and give the closest safe range. We accept the chair’s right to request the second written finding on a disputed or unresolved material issue.

We accept one hour from the maintenance lead’s determination as the target for making the relevant excerpt securely available to a preauthorized specialist. The lead may release it immediately and will log the question, recipient, excerpt and release time. Task-limited access, identifier protections and separate written authorization for firmware parameters apply as drafted. The board review period applies only to board materials. Repairs and safety notifications may proceed immediately.
